paras: The assault on Joe Hallier and B. L. Greer was an attack on 11 August 1903 at Horse Creek, Walker County, Alabama, in which armed white men beat Greer, the Black vice president of the Alabama district of the United Mine Workers, and shot Hallier, the union's white district organizer, in the arm. Both survived; six men were prosecuted in federal court for conspiracy, but a U.S. commissioner released them in October 1903 and a federal judge dismissed later indictments in May 1904 as a state matter. It drew notice because a white and a Black union officer were attacked together and because the prosecution turned on Hallier's citizenship.

On the night of 10 August the two men organized a small union local at Empire, about nine miles from Horse Creek, which was described as a non-union mining camp. They stopped at Horse Creek the next morning to take a train to Birmingham.

According to Greer's account in the first reports, five men headed by Charles Moore, superintendent of the Ivy Leaf mines, entered the depot and ordered the two at pistol point down the railroad track. Hallier testified in September that Moore asked whether "the negro" belonged with him, struck at him, fell, and drew a gun, while the others beat Greer over the head with their guns. Down the track, he said, Moore forced him at gunpoint to kiss Greer, called for a rope, and told him that "dead men tell no tales."

After the two were searched and ordered to trot, shots were fired, and a bullet passed through Hallier's upper arm and severed an artery. Greer stayed with him until a freight-train crew carried both to Birmingham, where Hallier was operated on at an infirmary. A hearing witness said he saw Chance, Moore, Ballinger and Patton following the two men and later found Hallier on the ties and Greer bleeding.
The Montgomery Advertiser reported "great indignation" among citizens and said Sheriff Frank Moore took deputies from Jasper to Horse Creek. Hallier was convalescent by 16 August.

Six men, Charley Moore, William Ballinger, John Chance, James E. DeLoach, R. B. Patton and Steve Smith, were charged before U.S. Commissioner H. A. Wilson with conspiracy against Hallier and placed under $2,000 bond. At the September hearing the district attorney conceded that the Welsh-born Hallier had not completed naturalization, and the government moved to add Greer to the affidavit. On 1 October Wilson allowed Greer's name but released the defendants, holding the evidence insufficient as to Greer and saying he would have bound them over had Hallier been shown a citizen.

A federal grand jury then indicted Moore, Ballinger, Chance, DeLoach and two Empire men, Luther Rabun and Sterling Shores, for conspiracy against Greer. In May 1904 Judge Thomas G. Jones sustained the defense demurrers and dismissed the case as an offense against Alabama law, not federal law. No report of a state prosecution was found.

The Birmingham Age-Herald broke the story on 12 August under "Joe Hallier Is Seriously Shot," while the Montgomery Advertiser ran it inside a column on the miners' arbitration hearing. Wire versions differed: the Indianapolis Journal's "Labor Leaders Mobbed" carried a subhead blaming the fact that a Black and a white man "Worked Together," while the New York Sun called it organizing "Resented With Violence." Weekly news digests as far away as Minnesota said Hallier was shot by "angry citizens" who objected to a union.

Alabama papers explained the attack by opposition to the union, and the Age-Herald followed the federal case, noting "much congratulation" among the defendants at their release. All coverage found was in white papers; no Black-press report was found.

The Indianapolis wire said "yesterday morning" under an 11 August dateline, but Hallier's testimony and later reports fix the attack on 11 August. Greer was quoted as saying the attackers were not miners, the Sun called them reportedly company employees, and the Age-Herald named a mine superintendent. The Advertiser had Hollier knock a man down, whereas Hallier testified that Moore swung first, and the Age-Herald put the wound in the left arm in August and the right in October.

reader.title: Assault on Joe Hallier and B. L. Greer
bases: Armed white men beat a Black and a white officer of the United Mine Workers and shot the white organizer the morning after the two organized a local at Empire, and every account explains the attack by opposition to the union (A4, A11, A18), with one headline adding the interracial partnership as cause (A1).

Independent same-day Birmingham and Montgomery reports (A3, A4), the wire (A1, A2), Hallier's sworn testimony and a defense-side witness at a federal hearing (A11, A13), and federal indictments (A19, A21) agree on the core assault and shooting.

accounts.label: Greer's account (first reports)
accounts.gist: Five men led by Moore entered the depot, marched them down the track at pistol point, forced Hallier to kiss Greer, beat Greer and fired on Hallier as he was made to trot.

accounts.label: Montgomery Advertiser special
accounts.gist: A 'posse of white men' beat Greer on the head at the depot; Hollier knocked down a man before both were driven out at pistol point, forced to run and fired on.

accounts.label: Hallier's sworn testimony
accounts.gist: Moore asked if he was organizing and if 'the negro' was with him, struck at him and fell; the others beat Greer with guns; Moore forced the kiss, threatened hanging and death, and shots were fired as they trotted.

accounts.label: Hearing witness
accounts.gist: A witness saw Chance, Moore, Ballinger and Patton following the two men, heard no shots, and later found Hallier lying on the ties and Greer bleeding.

accounts.label: Federal indictment
accounts.gist: The defendants conspired to injure and intimidate Greer to prevent him organizing a local in Walker County, assaulted and beat him, and assaulted him with intent to murder.

framing.detail: The Birmingham Age-Herald's 'Joe Hallier Is Seriously Shot' gave Greer's account, named a mine superintendent, and attributed the attack to opposition to unionizing Empire.
The Indianapolis Journal's 'Labor Leaders Mobbed' carried a subhead saying the attack was caused by a white and a Black man working together.
The Sun's 'Two Mine Workers Mobbed' framed it as an 'Effort to Organize a Non-Union Settlement Resented With Violence'.
The Montgomery Advertiser ran it as a sub-item in a column on the miners' arbitration hearing, reporting 'great indignation' among citizens.
Later Age-Herald reports followed the federal case, noting surprise in court and congratulation among defendants at their release and front-paging the 1904 dismissal.
